html:
How to package an application as a Helm 2 chart and deploy it into a namespace: what each file in the chart is for, when you need it, and how the pieces fit together into a complete, production-shaped release (image pull secret, ConfigMap, Secret, Service, Ingress, autoscaling, disruption budget and more).

Not tested yet. Written from Helm 2's documented behaviour. The chart is a complete, runnable example (myapp, which runs nginx) so every template can be shown in context. Run it once and fix anything that differs on your versions. It assumes the cluster and namespaces from Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind (or Create a local Kubernetes cluster with k3d).

Helm 2 is end-of-life (support ended in 2020) and Tiller, its in-cluster server, is a known security weak point (section 2.4). Use Helm 2 only because a project pins it. For a new project use Helm 3, which has no Tiller; section 11 lists the differences.

#1. How Helm 2 works

WordMeaning
ChartA folder of templates plus default settings: one application, packaged
ValuesThe settings that fill the templates: image tag, replicas, hostnames
TemplateA Kubernetes YAML file with {{ … }} holes that values fill in
ReleaseOne installed copy of a chart, with a name (web-prod). Install the same chart twice, get two releases
RevisionA numbered version of a release. Every upgrade makes a new one; rollback goes back to an old one
TillerThe server half of Helm 2. The client sends it the chart; Tiller renders it and applies it

Three consequences of Tiller to remember:

  • The client and Tiller must be the same Helm version, or Helm refuses with an "incompatible versions" error.
  • Tiller acts with its own ServiceAccount's permissions, not yours. Whatever it may do, anyone who can talk to it may do.
  • Tiller stores every release inside the cluster, as ConfigMaps in kube-system, including the values and the rendered manifests. See section 2.4 and section 8.

#2. Set up Helm 2 on your cluster

#2.1 The client

Pick the Helm 2 version to use and keep it the same everywhere (client and Tiller). This guide uses 2.17.0, the last Helm 2 release.

Native binary:

Client: v2.17.0+g…. On Apple Silicon this runs under Rosetta. Old Helm 2 builds are made with an old Go toolchain, and on some macOS versions they crash with a segmentation fault. If yours does, use the container version instead.

Container version (a Linux copy of the client, started per command). Create the kubeconfig it will use. It must use the cluster's address as seen from inside Docker's kind network, so it has its own file:

Do these in this order. If ~/.kube/kind-internal does not exist when Docker is asked to share it, Docker creates an empty folder with that name and everything after fails. (This container setup is for kind. On k3d, use the native binary.)

Then define a shell function (put it in ~/.zshrc to keep it):

Line by line:

  • docker run --rm -i — run Helm in a throwaway container.
  • --platform linux/amd64 — the image is Intel-only; Docker emulates it on Apple Silicon.
  • --network kind — join the network where the cluster's API server has the name the internal kubeconfig uses.
  • -v …kind-internal:/root/.kube/config:ro — hand Helm the kubeconfig, read-only.
  • -v ~/.helm2:/root/.helm — keep Helm's settings and repository cache between runs.
  • -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work — make the current folder visible inside, so helm2 install ./myapp finds your chart.
  • --entrypoint helm … "$@" — run helm with whatever arguments you typed.

Check that the image tag exists (docker pull lachlanevenson/k8s-helm:v2.17.0); any image that contains the Helm 2 client works the same way.

#2.2 Tiller: its account and its permission

This gives Tiller cluster-admin, which is the easy lab setup and the unsafe one (section 2.4).

#2.3 Install Tiller, matching the client version

Tiller's image is Intel-only too. On Apple Silicon, turn on Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation in Docker Desktop first.

Both lines must show the same version.

If helm2 init fails, you are probably on an older Helm 2 (2.10–2.14). Those describe Tiller as an extensions/v1beta1 Deployment, which modern Kubernetes removed. Have Helm print the description instead of applying it, rewrite it to apps/v1, and apply that with kubectl:

The perl part changes the API version and adds the selector that apps/v1 requires. Then finish the client side with helm2 init --client-only --stable-repo-url https://charts.helm.sh/stable.

#2.4 Tiller's security problem, and the habit that follows

  • Tiller with cluster-admin lets anyone who can reach it do anything in the cluster.
  • Release data is stored as ConfigMaps in kube-system, including your values. A secret passed to a chart can be read by anyone who may read ConfigMaps there.

The habit: do not put real secrets in values or in chart templates. Create them separately (section 8) and let the chart only reference them by name. A tighter setup (Tiller per namespace with a limited Role) exists but is more work; see the Helm 2 docs on "securing your Helm installation".

#3. What a chart is made of

Every file in templates/ that does not start with _ is rendered, and each document in it becomes a Kubernetes object. Files that render to nothing (a switched-off {{ if }}) are simply skipped.

#4. The template language in ten minutes

Templates are Go templates. Anything inside {{ }} is evaluated; the rest is copied as is.

Where values come from:

ExpressionValue
.Values.image.tagA setting from values.yaml, -f file or --set
.Release.NameThe name you gave the release
.Release.NamespaceThe namespace it is installed into
.Release.Revision1 for install, then 2, 3… on each upgrade
.Release.IsInstall / .Release.IsUpgradetrue on the matching operation
.Release.ServiceTiller in Helm 2
.Chart.Name, .Chart.Version, .Chart.AppVersionFrom Chart.yaml
.Template.BasePathThe templates/ folder, for including another file
.Files.Get "files/app.conf"The text of a file in the chart
.Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "x/v1"Whether the cluster supports an API

What to do with them:

SyntaxMeaning
{{ .Values.x | quote }}Pipe a value through a function, here wrapping it in quotes
{{ default "a" .Values.x }}Use "a" if x is empty
{{ required "x is required" .Values.x }}Stop with an error if x is empty
{{ if .Values.x }} … {{ else }} … {{ end }}Conditional
{{ range $k, $v := .Values.map }} … {{ end }}Loop
{{ with .Values.x }} … {{ end }}Run only if set, and make . mean x inside
{{ toYaml .Values.x | indent 8 }}Turn a value into YAML and indent it 8 spaces
{{ include "myapp.fullname" . }}Run a named snippet from _helpers.tpl
{{ printf "%s-%s" a b }}Build a string
{{ .Values.x | b64enc }}, sha256sum, trunc 63Encode, hash, shorten

Two details that cause most template bugs:

  • {{- and -}} trim whitespace on that side, including newlines. {{- if … }} removes the line break before it, which keeps the output free of blank lines.
  • Inside range and with, . changes. To reach the top-level values from inside, save what you need first ({{- $fullName := include "myapp.fullname" . -}}) or use $ (the root).

Helm 2 limits. There is no lookup function (Helm 3 only). Use indent, not nindent (older Helm 2 versions do not have it). A release name may be at most 53 characters.

#5. Build the chart, file by file

Start in the folder where you keep your work:

#5.1 Chart.yaml: the chart's identity

  • apiVersion: v1 — Helm 2 charts use v1. v2 is for Helm 3 charts and Helm 2 rejects it.
  • name — the chart's name; must match the folder.
  • version — the version of the chart (bump it when you change the templates).
  • appVersion — the version of the application inside (informational).

#5.2 values.yaml: every setting in one place

The defaults for everything the templates read. A chart with a good values.yaml needs no template edits for a new environment.

The rule behind the layout: every behaviour a team might want to change is a value, and every optional object has an enabled (or create) switch so it can be turned off without editing a template.

#5.3 templates/_helpers.tpl: names and labels, defined once

A file starting with _ renders nothing. It holds named snippets that the other templates call with include. Without it, every template would repeat the same naming and label logic.

What each snippet gives you:

  • myapp.fullname — the name used for every object: <release>-<chart> (cut to 63 characters, the Kubernetes limit). Two releases of the same chart in one namespace never collide, because the release name differs.
  • myapp.selectorLabels — the two labels that identify this release's pods. The Deployment's selector and the Service's selector both use exactly these. They must never change after the first install: a Deployment's selector cannot be edited.
  • myapp.labels — the selector labels plus the standard descriptive ones (app.kubernetes.io/…), put on every object so kubectl get all -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=<release> finds the whole release.
  • myapp.serviceAccountName / myapp.secretName — "the one this chart created, or the one the user named".

#5.4 serviceaccount.yaml: the pod's identity

  • Pods use the namespace's shared default account unless told otherwise. A dedicated account per app means its permissions (if any) can be set per app. See Users and permissions: who may do what, in which namespace.
  • automountServiceAccountToken: false stops Kubernetes from putting an API token inside the pod. An app that never calls the API should not have one.
  • The file also shows the standard pattern: {{- if … }} wraps the whole object, so one value switches it on or off.
  • To give the app API permissions, add a role.yaml (a Role) and rolebinding.yaml for this account.

#5.5 imagepullsecret.yaml: the registry login (regsecret)

Needed only when the image lives in a private registry. The public images (nginx, redis) and the local registry from Run your own image in the cluster need none. A pod that cannot pull shows ImagePullBackOff, with pull access denied in kubectl describe pod.

regsecret is simply the conventional name for this Secret. Its type is kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, and it holds a Docker login.

The recommended way is to create it outside the chart (so the password never enters a release record):

Then the chart only needs the name: --set imagePullSecret.name=regsecret.

If the chart must create it, this template builds it from values:

and a helper that builds the JSON. Add it to _helpers.tpl:

How the pod uses it: the Deployment (5.8) lists imagePullSecrets: - name: regsecret. Alternatively, attach it to the ServiceAccount once, and every pod using that account gets it automatically.

Careful: a password with a " in it breaks the JSON above, and the password ends up in the release record (section 2.4). That is why kubectl create secret docker-registry is the better choice.

#5.6 configmap.yaml: settings

For settings that are not secret: log level, feature flags, URLs, whole config files.

Two ConfigMaps, for two ways to deliver settings:

  • As environment variables. The first one holds key/value pairs from values.yaml; the Deployment loads them all with envFrom. Quote every value (| quote): environment variables are strings, and a bare true or 8080 would be rendered as a boolean or number and rejected.
  • As files. The second holds a whole file read from the chart (.Files.Get), which the Deployment mounts as a file. Keep it separate from the first: a key like app.conf is not a valid environment variable name.

A ConfigMap change does not restart pods by itself. The Deployment (5.8) carries a checksum of the ConfigMap in an annotation, so a changed ConfigMap changes the pod template, which makes Kubernetes roll the pods.

#5.7 secret.yaml: credentials

  • stringData takes plain text and lets the API server store it encoded. (Under data you would have to base64-encode each value yourself.)
  • The chart only creates the Secret when secret.create is true and no existingSecret is named. The recommended pattern is the opposite: create the Secret yourself (section 8) and set secret.existingSecret=<name>, so the credentials never pass through Helm.
  • A base64 Secret is not encrypted, only encoded. Protect it with permissions (Users and permissions: who may do what, in which namespace) and, on a real cluster, encryption at rest.
  • Do not generate random passwords in the template (randAlphaNum): every upgrade would generate a new one and Helm 2 has no lookup to read the old one.

#5.8 deployment.yaml: the application

The most important file. It keeps N copies of your container running and replaces them safely on change.

What each part does:

  • apiVersion: apps/v1 — the current API for Deployments. Older charts say extensions/v1beta1 or apps/v1beta1, which modern Kubernetes removed. apps/v1 also requires selector.
  • replicas is left out when the autoscaler is on. If both set it, every upgrade would reset the count the autoscaler chose.
  • selector.matchLabels — how the Deployment recognises its pods. It must match the pod template's labels and, once created, cannot be changed.
  • strategy — maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 means "start one new pod, wait until it is ready, then stop one old pod": an update never drops below the full count.
  • checksum/config, checksum/secret — hashes of those two files inside the pod template. Change a ConfigMap or Secret value and the hash changes, the pod template changes, and Kubernetes rolls the pods so they pick up the new settings.
  • imagePullSecrets — the registry login from 5.5, only when a name is set.
  • podSecurityContext / securityContext — run as non-root, drop privileges, read-only filesystem. Empty by default because it depends on the image; for an app you control, set runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and drop all capabilities.
  • image — repository:tag. required makes the install fail with a clear message if no tag was given. Use a specific tag (1.27, a commit hash), never latest.
  • env — the POD_NAME entry shows valueFrom: fieldRef, a value Kubernetes fills in (pod name, namespace, node name); the loop adds plain entries from values.env. To take a single key from a Secret, use valueFrom: secretKeyRef: {name: …, key: …}.
  • envFrom — loads every key of the ConfigMap and the Secret as environment variables. optional: true lets the pod start when the Secret does not exist yet.
  • livenessProbe — "is it stuck?" On failure, Kubernetes restarts the container.
  • readinessProbe — "can it take traffic?" On failure, the pod is taken out of the Service, not restarted. This is what makes rolling updates safe. (A startupProbe, for slow-starting apps, holds off the other two until the first start succeeds.)
  • resources — requests is what the scheduler reserves for the pod; limits is the ceiling. Without requests, autoscaling by CPU does not work. A pod over its memory limit is killed; over its CPU limit it is slowed down.
  • volumeMounts / volumes — the files ConfigMap mounted as a read-only folder, and optionally the persistent volume from 5.13.
  • nodeSelector, affinity, tolerations — placement, as in Deploy apps into your namespaces, one at a time and Concepts: what each piece is. Spread the replicas over nodes with a pod anti-affinity rule, passed as a value:
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds — how long a pod gets to finish in-flight requests after it is told to stop. Raise it for slow shutdowns.

Namespaces: none of these files sets metadata.namespace. The namespace comes from helm install --namespace web, so the same chart installs anywhere.

#5.9 service.yaml: a stable name for the pods

  • selector — the same selector labels as the Deployment. This is how the Service finds the pods.
  • port — the Service's port. targetPort: http — the container port by name (http from the Deployment), so the number lives in one place.
  • type — ClusterIP (inside the cluster only), NodePort (a fixed port on every node), LoadBalancer (an external address from the cloud or from k3d's load balancer).
  • Other pods reach it as <release>-myapp (same namespace) or <release>-myapp.<namespace>.

#5.10 ingress.yaml: HTTP routing from outside

Needs an ingress controller in the cluster (k3d bundles Traefik; on kind install one).

  • networking.k8s.io/v1 is the current API (Kubernetes 1.19 and later). The older extensions/v1beta1 and networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 Ingresses are removed from current clusters. To support old and new clusters, branch on .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "networking.k8s.io/v1".
  • $fullName and $svcPort are saved at the top because . changes meaning inside the range loops.
  • tls names a Secret holding the certificate (type kubernetes.io/tls), created by hand or by cert-manager.
  • annotations carry controller-specific settings, for example nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size.

#5.11 hpa.yaml: autoscaling the pods

  • Adds pods when average CPU use passes the target (a percentage of the pod's CPU request, so requests are required), and removes them when it falls.
  • Needs metrics-server (bundled with k3s; install it on kind).
  • autoscaling/v2 needs Kubernetes 1.23 or later; on older clusters use autoscaling/v2beta2.
  • This is pod autoscaling. Adding nodes is a different system.

#5.12 pdb.yaml: stay available during maintenance

When someone drains a node (kubectl drain, an upgrade), Kubernetes evicts its pods. A PodDisruptionBudget says "never take me below this many pods": a drain waits instead of evicting the last healthy copy. It only helps with more than one replica; with minAvailable: 1 and one replica, a drain would block forever. Needs Kubernetes 1.21 or later for policy/v1.

#5.13 pvc.yaml: storage that outlives the pod

A claim asks the cluster for a disk. ReadWriteOnce means one node at a time. In a lab, the default storage class (bundled in k3s and kind) hands out a local directory. With several replicas and ReadWriteOnce, use a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates instead, so each pod gets its own disk (see the end of this section).

#5.14 networkpolicy.yaml: who may talk to the pods

By default every pod can reach every other pod. This allows traffic to the app's port only from other pods in the same namespace and drops the rest. Add another from entry (namespaceSelector) for an ingress controller in a different namespace. It does nothing unless the cluster's network plugin enforces policies (see Users and permissions: who may do what, in which namespace).

#5.15 job-migrate.yaml: a hook that runs before each install or upgrade

A hook is an object Helm runs at a point in the release's life, instead of installing it with the rest. The classic use is a database migration.

  • helm.sh/hook: pre-install,pre-upgrade — run it before the rest is created or changed. Others: post-install, post-upgrade, pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test-success.
  • hook-weight — the order among several hooks (lowest first).
  • hook-delete-policy — hook-succeeded removes the Job when it finishes OK; before-hook-creation removes an old copy first so a repeat run does not collide.
  • Helm waits for the hook Job to finish. If it fails, the install or upgrade fails and nothing else is changed.
  • A pre-install hook runs before the chart's ConfigMap and Secret exist. If the job needs them, create them first (section 8), or mark those objects as hooks with a lower weight.

#5.16 cronjob.yaml: a scheduled task

Runs a container on a schedule (cron syntax). concurrencyPolicy: Forbid skips a run if the previous one is still going. batch/v1 needs Kubernetes 1.21 or later.

#5.17 NOTES.txt: what to tell the user after install

Printed by helm install and helm status. Not a Kubernetes object.

#5.18 tests/test-connection.yaml: a built-in check

A pod that only runs when you type helm2 test <release>. If it exits successfully the test passes. It proves the Service resolves and answers.

#5.19 .helmignore

Files listed here are left out when the chart is packaged. Same idea as .gitignore.

#5.20 requirements.yaml: other charts you depend on

If your app needs Redis or Postgres, depend on their charts instead of writing them:

Downloads the dependency into myapp/charts/. condition: redis.enabled lets a user switch it off with a value. Settings for the dependency go under its name in your values (redis: {…}). Helm 2 uses requirements.yaml next to Chart.yaml; Helm 3 puts dependencies inside Chart.yaml.

#5.21 Other objects you may add

FileWhen you need it
statefulset.yamlThe app needs a stable identity and its own disk per pod (databases, queues): pods are named name-0, name-1, … and each gets a volume from volumeClaimTemplates. Replaces deployment.yaml, and needs a headless Service (clusterIP: None) named in serviceName
role.yaml + rolebinding.yamlThe app itself calls the Kubernetes API (a controller, an operator). Grant only the verbs it uses to the chart's ServiceAccount
daemonset.yamlOne pod on every node (log shippers, node monitors)
servicemonitor.yamlYou run Prometheus Operator and want the app's metrics scraped
resourcequota.yaml, limitrange.yamlUsually not in an app chart: they belong to the namespace, set once by whoever owns the cluster
CRDs in crds/Helm 2 has no special CRD handling (Helm 3 adds a crds/ folder). Install CRDs separately

#7. Install, upgrade, roll back, remove

Make sure web exists (kubectl get ns web) and that kubectl config current-context is your lab cluster.

Install:

  • myapp — the chart folder. --name demo — the release name. --namespace web — where to put it.
  • Prints the objects it created, then NOTES.txt.

Everything belonging to this release, found through the labels from _helpers.tpl.

Test it:

Upgrade — change an image tag or a setting, and Helm makes revision 2:

  • --wait — do not return until the pods are ready. --timeout 300 — give up after 300 seconds.
  • Settings you do not repeat go back to the chart's defaults, unless you add --reuse-values. This surprises everyone once. Keep your settings in files (section 9) and pass them every time.

The command to use in a pipeline: install if new, upgrade if it exists:

Add --atomic to roll back automatically if the upgrade fails.

Remove it:

Deletes every object and the release record. Without --purge, Helm 2 keeps the record and the name cannot be reused.

#8. Secrets and credentials: keep them out of the release

Helm 2 stores each release, including its values, as a ConfigMap in kube-system. So:

Create credentials yourself, once, outside Helm:

Point the chart at them by name:

The chart then carries only names, never values. Rotating a password means updating the Secret and restarting the pods (kubectl rollout restart deployment/demo-myapp -n web).

For team use, keep Secrets in git encrypted, with Sealed Secrets, SOPS or an external secrets operator that syncs from a vault. Never commit a plain values-secret.yaml.

#9. One chart, many environments

The same chart deploys every environment; only the values change. One file per environment, in git:

Which value wins (last one beats earlier ones): the chart's values.yaml, then each -f file in the order given, then --set. So the order is defaults → environment file → the one value the pipeline sets.

#10. A checklist for "a perfect system"

AreaDo this
Naming and labelsOne fullname helper; the standard app.kubernetes.io/* labels on every object; never edit selector labels after the first install
ImageA specific tag or commit hash, never latest; a private registry uses imagePullSecrets (regsecret) created outside the chart
HealthA readinessProbe and a livenessProbe on every container
Resourcesrequests and limits on every container; autoscaling needs requests
AvailabilityAt least 2 replicas, a rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0, a PodDisruptionBudget, anti-affinity to spread over nodes
ConfigNon-secret settings in a ConfigMap; a checksum annotation so config changes roll the pods
SecretsCreated outside the chart, referenced by name; existingSecret pattern; encrypted in git
IdentityA ServiceAccount per app; no API token unless the app calls the API; a Role only if it does
SecurityrunAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities; Pod Security labels on the namespace
NetworkA NetworkPolicy that allows only the traffic the app needs
DataA migration hook (or init step) before the new version starts; PVCs or a StatefulSet for state
OperationsNOTES.txt; a helm test; helm lint and helm template in CI; --atomic or --wait; per-environment values files in git
Portabilityapps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1 and similar current APIs; no hard-coded namespace; .Capabilities checks if you must support old clusters

#11. Helm 2 versus Helm 3

Helm 2Helm 3
Server in the clusterTiller (needs install, RBAC, version match)None: Helm uses your own kubeconfig and permissions
Release records stored inConfigMaps in kube-systemSecrets in the release's own namespace
Release namesGlobal, unique across the clusterPer namespace
Chart.yaml apiVersionv1, dependencies in requirements.yamlv2, dependencies inside Chart.yaml
Installhelm install ./chart --name xhelm install x ./chart
Deletehelm delete x --purgehelm uninstall x
Template function lookupnoyes
CRDsno special supporta crds/ folder

To move a running Helm 2 setup over, use the helm 2to3 plugin, which converts releases in place.

#12. When something goes wrong

MessageCause and fix
Error: could not find tillerTiller's pod is not ready: kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy/tiller-deploy
Error: incompatible versions client[…] server[…]Client and Tiller differ. Reinstall one so both match (section 2)
Error: no available release name foundTiller is reachable but has a problem, often its ServiceAccount permissions: recheck 2.2
Error: a release named demo already existsUse helm2 upgrade --install, or helm2 delete demo --purge first
Error: UPGRADE FAILED: "demo" has no deployed releasesThe first install failed and left a record: helm2 delete demo --purge, then install again
error converting YAML to JSON / did not find expected keyIndentation or whitespace wrong in a template. Run helm2 template and read the output at the line number
no matches for kind "X" in version "…"The template uses an API version your cluster does not have (or no longer has). Use a current one (5.8, 5.10)
field is immutable / selector error on upgradeYou changed the Deployment's selector. Delete the Deployment (helm2 delete --purge) and install again
Pods ImagePullBackOffWrong image or tag; private registry without regsecret; a local image not loaded (Run your own image in the cluster)
Pods CreateContainerConfigErrorA referenced ConfigMap or Secret key is missing; kubectl describe pod names it
helm2: segmentation faultThe native Helm 2 binary crashes on your OS: use the container version (2.1)
~/.kube/kind-internal is a directoryDocker made a folder because the file was missing: rmdir it, create the file, retry (2.1)

#13. Clean up

To remove Tiller itself:

Deleting the whole cluster (Stop, shut down and clean up) removes all of it, Tiller included.
